reader.title: Killing of Thomas Edmondson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The only lynching content is the wire's report that after Gick's arrest for shooting Edmondson there was difficulty restraining people from lynching him; no attack on him is reported, and the killing itself was a shooting by three men, not a mob (A1, A4, A2).

No one was lynched: the crowd's threat against Gick was restrained, and he was tried, convicted and sentenced to life (A1, A9, A10); Edmondson was shot by Gick and two companions, a killing the papers describe as an assassination over a grudge, not a killing under the pretext of justice (A2, A3).

Several separately written reports agree that Edmondson was shot at Good Hope and Gick was arrested (A1, A2, A3, A6), and a later conviction and sentence are reported (A9, A10); the lynching threat itself appears only in one wire text (A1, A4, A5, A8).

summary.text: The killing of Thomas Edmondson was the fatal shooting of a citizen of Good Hope, a village near Macomb, Illinois, on the night of Friday, March 17, 1882, by three men he had earlier turned over to the police.
The accused gunman, Ed. Gick, was arrested, and a Chicago dispatch reported that people were restrained only with difficulty from lynching him.
Gick was convicted of murder that September, and the judge's handling of his sentence caused an outcry in McDonough County.
Edmondson was described as "a prominent citizen" and, in other reports, as "an old and highly-respected citizen" of Good Hope.
According to the Chicago dispatch, a few days before his death he had turned three "roughs" over to the police for "improper conduct."
The New-York Tribune said he had arrested the men himself.
On Friday night the three men shot Edmondson dead, and the dispatch named Gick as the one who fired.
A separate item in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer said he was shot three times by "a young man named Gick" and died almost at once, and it attributed the killing to "an old grudge."
Gick was arrested, while the other two men escaped.
After the arrest, the longer version of the wire reported, "there was difficulty in restraining people from lynching him."
None of the reports describes an attack on Gick or says who held the crowd back, and no report gives the race of anyone involved.
Gick, named in the court report as Robert E. Gick, was convicted at Macomb on September 29, 1882, of Edmondson's murder.
According to State's Attorney William Prentiss, the jury fixed the penalty at death, but Judge Shope pressed the prosecution for days to accept a life sentence instead.

Prentiss wrote that Edmondson's widow wanted the verdict to stand, but after the judge suggested that the record held grounds for a new trial, the prosecution consented to set the verdict aside on condition that Gick plead guilty to wilful murder.
Gick then pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life in the penitentiary.

The change from hanging to life confinement, the Canton Register reported, "aroused great popular indignation throughout McDonough County," and Prentiss attacked the judge in a card in the Macomb Journal.

The killing reached papers outside Illinois mainly through a Chicago dispatch dated March 19, which the St. Paul Daily Globe ran as "Assassinated by Hoodlums" and the Salt Lake Herald and Cheyenne Daily Leader carried in crime columns.
The Northern Pacific Farmer of Wadena, Minnesota, reprinted the same text on March 23 in a column headed "Crimes."
Only this longer version mentioned the threat of lynching.

Shorter items dropped it: the New-York Tribune's "Assassinated by Ruffians" ended with the escape of Gick's companions, and a "Tragical Tales" roundup in the Mower County Transcript and Watertown Republican dated the shooting to the night of the 18th.
The papers framed the case as a crime against a respectable man by "roughs" and "ruffians," and the later Illinois coverage centered on the sentence rather than the threatened lynching.
Most reports, including the conviction notice, called the victim Thomas Edmondson, while the St. Paul copy of the wire gave his initials as "E. S."
The dispatches dated March 19 placed the shooting on Friday night, March 17, against the 18th in a weekly roundup, and the dispatches are the closer source.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Chicago wire in crime roundups under 'Assassinated by Hoodlums', 'Criminalities' or 'Crime Record', calling the victim a 'prominent citizen' and the killers 'roughs'.
Shorter items ('Assassinated by Ruffians', 'Result of an Old Grudge', 'Tragical Tales') dropped the lynching sentence entirely.
The Canton Register reprinted the State's Attorney's attack on the judge for sparing Gick the gallows, under 'An Indignant Prosecuting Attorney'.

conflicts.note: Most reports, including the conviction notice, use Thomas; 'E. S.' appears only in the St. Paul copy of the wire and its reprint.
The dispatches dated March 19 say Friday; the 18th appears only in a weekly roundup.

record_check.dossier: A murder by three men followed by a restrained lynching threat against the arrested shooter; no race is reported for anyone, so nothing marks it as anti-Black
threatened at most; Gick was not taken and was later tried and sentenced
Only Thomas Edmondson was killed; 'Ed. Click' is a misreading of Ed. Gick, the accused shooter, who was threatened but not harmed
Edmondson's killers were three named-in-part 'roughs' (Gick and two who escaped); the 'people' who threatened Gick are unnamed and of unstated number

Good Hope, a village near Macomb ('Macombville'), Illinois
Thomas Edmondson (Edmundson, Edmonson; 'E. S. Edmondson' in one wire version), a 'prominent' or 'respected' citizen, shot dead; race not stated
Ed. Gick (Geck, Giek; Robert E. Gick at conviction) accused of firing the shots that killed Edmondson
